faq.q: What is the voice coil in a speaker?
faq.a: It is a light coil of wire glued to the back of the cone. The music signal flows through it, turning it into an electromagnet whose strength and direction change with the sound.
asks: What does the coil in a speaker do?

faq.q: Why does a speaker have a magnet?
faq.a: The fixed magnet pushes and pulls the voice coil whenever current flows through it. Without it, the coil would have nothing to push against.
asks: What is the magnet in a speaker for?

faq.q: How does the cone make sound?
faq.a: The cone moves in and out with the coil, squashing and stretching the air in front of it. Those pressure waves travel to your ear as sound.

faq.q: How does a speaker make high and low notes?
faq.a: A low note moves the cone in and out slowly, perhaps 50 times a second; a high note moves it thousands of times a second. Big woofers handle bass and small tweeters handle treble.
asks: What is a woofer and a tweeter?

faq.q: Why does a speaker need an amplifier?
faq.a: The signal from a phone or player is very weak. An amplifier boosts it into a current strong enough to drive the coil and move the cone hard.

facts: Humans can hear sounds from roughly 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second.
The moving-coil loudspeaker design still used today was developed by Chester Rice and Edward Kellogg in the 1920s.
